deep.reconstruction: This page continues Euler's table, begun on p.112, for every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) from 101 to 421. Each row gives the unique decomposition p = b² + c² and the residue class a ≡ ±r (mod p), with 0 < r < p/2, of all numbers a for which p divides a² + 1. In modern terms r is the square root of −1 modulo p. Scholion 1 on the preceding page describes how Euler obtains it: from p = b² + c², every a ≡ ±b·c⁻¹ (mod p) gives a² + 1 ≡ 0, because b² ≡ −c². Example: 109 = 3² + 10², and 33 ≡ 10·3⁻¹ (mod 109) since 3·33 = 99 ≡ −10, and 33² = 1089 = 10·109 − 1. The table serves the paper's aim of deciding which numbers aa + 1 are prime even when they are very large. Any odd prime divisor of a² + 1 is ≡ 1 (mod 4) and must divide it for a in one of these two classes. So, with the table, one can strike out composite values of a² + 1 by a sieve over arithmetic progressions instead of dividing each value by every candidate prime. This is a sieve of Eratosthenes adapted to the quadratic polynomial x² + 1, and it is the basis for Euler's later list of a for which a² + 1 is prime.
errors: None found on this page. I checked all 29 rows: each p is the correct sum of two squares, each r satisfies r² ≡ −1 (mod p), and each r is the least such residue. Examples: 107² = 11449 = 50·229 − 1; 138² = 19044 = 65·293 − 1; 148² = 21904 = 65·337 − 1; 143² = 20449 = 50·409 − 1. The list of primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) between 101 and 421 is complete.

ideas.what: Square roots of −1 modulo p obtained from the two-square representation p = b² + c² as a ≡ ±b/c (mod p)
ideas.modern_name: Computing √−1 mod p from Fermat's two-square decomposition (Gaussian-integer factorisation p = (b+ci)(b−ci))
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (two-square theory, 1740s–1750s); systematised by Lagrange and Gauss; tabulated by Jacobi (Canon arithmeticus, 1839) and Cunningham
ideas.where_published: E283 (Novi Comm. 9, 1764), Scholion 1–2 and this table; Euler's two-square papers E228/E241

ideas.what: Table of the residue classes a mod p with p | a² + 1, used to sieve the values a² + 1 for primality
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic sieve for primes of the form n² + 1 (Landau's fourth problem)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, E283 (well known in histories, e.g. Dickson's History, vol. I)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a correct, routine computational table belonging to a well-known paper whose method is documented in Dickson and elsewhere. Nothing on the page is new.
